title: Between the testaments
hookLine: the quieter centuries: Greek rule, then Rome, synagogues everywhere, and people waiting

lines: MALACHI: I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH.
cards: Open a King James Bible printed without the Apocrypha, turn to the last page of the Old Testament, and you land in Malachi.

Its final verses look forward: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." Turn one page, and you're in Matthew, with a family tree and a baby.
In your hands it's one page. In history it's a long stretch, the gap between the two testaments. Some readers call them the silent years.
But they weren't silent. They were waiting years.

teach.b: First Maccabees opens with Alexander the Great sweeping through and Greek kings ruling the land after him; yesterday's rededicated temple happens in those years. Then Rome arrives.

Luke's account of the birth opens with an emperor: "there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Meanwhile something quieter grows: the synagogue, a gathering for reading and prayer.
In Acts, James says "Moses of old time hath in every city them that preach him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath day."
And in Nazareth, Luke says of Jesus, "as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day." A custom, going on long enough to become habit. Through it all, people wait.

Simeon, a man in Jerusalem, "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel." And Anna, a prophet who never left the temple, who spoke of the child "to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem."
Waiting, in these pages, isn't doing nothing. It's showing up, reading, praying, keeping the customs, for years, without seeing what you're waiting for.
Paul, writing later as a follower of Jesus, looks back: "when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son." Some readers hear in that word something filling slowly.

And this closes a long run, from Joshua at the Jordan through judges and kings, Ruth and Samuel, David and Solomon, Elijah and Elisha, the fall and the exile, Esther, Ezra and Nehemiah, to people standing in the temple, waiting.

how: Some Christians meet the years between the testaments through the people waiting at the start of the Gospels, like Simeon and Anna, and churches that keep Advent take up that same waiting in the weeks before Christmas.

games.q: you're Simeon, just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel. nothing has happened yet. what do you do today?
o: give up. it's been too long.
stop waiting and make it happen yourself.
games.why: Simeon keeps coming. Luke says he came by the Spirit into the temple on the day Mary and Joseph brought the child.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for: news, healing, a reconciliation, a change in the world or in yourself.

Don't hurry it and don't give up on it; hold it the way Simeon might have, showing up one more day, and let your breath slow down around it. If you pray, bring that waiting to God; if you don't, just keep it company.

wordCard.voice: Simeon. A man in Jerusalem waiting for the consolation of Israel, one face of the long stretch between Malachi and Matthew.

carryVoice: Your line: the waiting years. That closes this part of the path, Joshua to the return; next, the early church. Day seven hundred forty-six, done.
